correctness.rationale: For t=p/(1-p)>0, stripping the factor (1-p)^n produces b_j=sum_{floor(2k/3)=j} choose(n,k)t^k on contiguous support. The first gap factors as t^3[C(n,2)^2t-(1+nt)(C(n,3)+C(n,4)t)]. At n=3 and n=4 the first gap is the only interior one; at n=5 the remaining gap factors as 5t^6(5t^2+18t+20)>0. Solving the first three low-n polynomials and converting odds to probabilities yields the stated closed intervals. At n=6 its first gap requires 1/3<=t<=2/3, while the fourth-to-fifth tail gap t^9(21t-20) forces t>=20/21, impossible. At n>=7 the discriminant is -n^2(n-1)^2(5n^4-42n^3+73n^2-36n-12)/192, with its parenthesis equal to a strictly positive polynomial at n=7+m; the downward quadratic is everywhere negative. The argument proves the infinite cutoff, not merely grid evidence. Independently verified the discriminant and 1200 exact rational binomial mass comparisons.
residual_risks: Only ordinary log-concavity of the exact floor map, not ultra-log-concavity or the whole Poisson-binomial class.
Degenerate endpoint probabilities p=0,1 are excluded and would be trivially log-concave.

value.rationale: Log-concavity is a natural discrete shape property tied to unimodality, estimation and negative-dependence hierarchies. A rational floor quantizer can destroy it despite binomial ultra-log-concavity; the finding gives an exact full phase diagram, algebraic boundary windows and a sharp six-trial universal obstruction. This completes a motivated natural classification for a quantizer singled out in prior work; it is not just a table of a few examples or a trivial failure of real-rootedness.
residual_risks: Scope fixed to homogeneous binomial and slope 2/3; extension to other rational slopes would require fresh arguments.
